C2.1: Closing a low-pass filter turns a buzzy saw into a round, dark bass, and opening it again brings the bite back.
C2.2: Turning up resonance makes a filter sweep squelch and whistle, the sound behind wet, rubbery basslines.
C2.3: Choosing high-pass, band-pass or notch lets you thin a pad so it leaves room for the bass, or carve a narrow, nasal lead.
C2.4: A steep filter shuts a bass down hard and dark, while a gentle one leaves some edge, so you pick what the track needs.
C2.5: Driving a sound into the filter adds grit and thickness, giving you a warm, heavy bass or a harsh, snarling one.
C2.6: Letting the cutoff follow the keys keeps a bassline or melody equally bright from its lowest note to its highest.
C2.7: Ringing a filter until it whistles gives you eerie, glassy tones you can play as melodies from the keyboard.
C2.C: Naming what a filter has taken away by ear lets you copy the dark, squelchy or gritty tone of a sound you hear.
C3.1: Shaping how a note starts, settles and fades decides whether your sound stabs, swells or lingers after you lift your finger.
C3.2: With only four controls you can turn the same oscillators into a short pluck for a melody, a slow pad or a steady organ.
C3.3: Keeping a note at full level for a moment gives a bass hit more weight up front, and the fall shape makes it sound struck.
C3.4: An envelope on the cutoff gives each bass note a bright start that closes down, the plucky movement that makes a bassline bounce.
C3.5: Sending an envelope to pitch builds a kick that thumps, a laser zap for a fill, or a lead that scoops up into each note.
C3.6: On a high-pass the body of a note arrives late, and on a band-pass it speaks like a vowel, handy for odd, talking basses.
C3.C: Judging how a sound starts, holds, fades and changes brightness lets you match the timing of a pluck, pad or bass by ear.
